utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Prelec.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, good morning, and let us resume where we left off yesterday. You explained to us this system that was put in place at the time when you -- while you were expecting documents in Samobor, that is HIS documents and a system of reciprocity. You mentioned the example when you were given two boxes and that you could pick up any one of them because they were identical, and will you please say do you know what I'm talking about, because I have a question about this. The system of reciprocity, that is the Office for Cooperation of the Croatian government with the Tribunal and that the manager of that system, of that inspection, this system of reciprocity was in force only while you were in Samobor and worked there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this system of reciprocity did not apply to the later stage of your work at the state archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please wait for the end of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are being asked by the interpreters for the pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I was sure I was slow enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It was the witness who was, in fact, being reminded. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, it's my fault anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prelec, are you sure that the system of reciprocity did not apply any longer when you were at the state archives?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- I personally assumed that it was continuing and I only discovered after some time that it was not. I have no reason to believe that the system of reciprocity, to use your term, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we agree. And my next question about the same topic: Could you give us a rough estimate, an order of magnitude regarding the volume of the documents at the Samobor at the first stage compared with the state archive as the second stage, the two separate stages. At which of these two stages did you get more documents in terms of their volume?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without question, the materials copied at the Croatian State Archive were much greater in quantity than the other materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I know that you wouldn't have a figure, but just as a description, was it 1:2, 1:3 roughly, just a rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say at least 10:1. It's possible to construct a precise answer, but not on the basis of information I have at my fingertips now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I agree with you it is impossible to know it very precisely. You say 10:1, which means ten documents, of course order of magnitude, ten documents in the state archives versus one document in Samobor; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were there much longer, and we became more efficient, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Yesterday you explained to us that small state archive stamp in the right upper corner of those documents, and you told us, and you will correct me if I'm wrong, that this stamp can be found on almost all the documents in the state archive, even if not on all of them. But I didn't quite understand from what you told us again what was the ratio. I know that you cannot give us the exact figure, but what are we talking about? Is the stamp a rule and then there are only exceptions to this rule, or could you tell us roughly what proportion of documents did have a stamp and which proportion didn't?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to say at least 2 or 3 to 1, probably more. But again, a precise answer could be established but not by me right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But from everything that you told us, we can agree that the majority of documents that you obtained in the archive has a seal, a stamp?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that the state archive began gradually to sort the documents out, and you told us that, in the beginning, there were very modest groups of binders or boxes or folders or lists but that they all grew in time. I should like to put to you that the list drawn up by the state archive at no time reached a stage when individual documents would be identified. They never got beyond the listing of or identifying individual bunches of documents, that is as per binder or folder, and categorise them according to subject or author or something like that, but it never came down to every individual document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exception, that being items which had a very small number of large documents. For example, the logbooks and what was called the Blaskic diary colloquially yesterday, those were listed individually. But that would be the only exception I'm aware of, those kinds of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me try to be clearer. And even this exception was not the product of the work of the archive but the nature of the document, because this accurate itemisation was due to the nature of the document itself rather than a system developed by the archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both are correct. It's the nature of the document but they were written down by the archive. So it seems to be a false alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. Never mind. But we agree that that is the only exception, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only one of which I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to be on the safe side, the last day that you went to the archive, was there at least in one part of it one of the -- one of the binders, say, the Vitez Brigade, covering its existence? Is there an accurate, an exhaustive list of documents collected, put together in one binder, on the last day that you were at the archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a qualification. In some of the materials I referred to yesterday relating to investigations carried out by the SIS on behalf of what was referred to as the Defence, there were lists of document numbers but they were not in any way identified, and they were quite long, and I did not try to establish whether they corresponded with any particular binder. That would have been an enormously time-intensive and difficult task. But this is probably not what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, of course not. Thank you. And as for this classification of documents, one more question. You or your colleagues who worked with you, I'd like to put it to you that you never saw a binder or a folder containing documents of the Vitez Brigade and where there would be, at the beginning of the binder, a list of documents included in that particular binder or folder; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any such lists, but please keep in mind that the Viteska Brigade's documents I saw in May and other parts of that collection at other times. So my recollection might not be perfect, but I don't recall any such lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you testified about document Z692.2, if you remember. I have to ask the usher to help us, please. It is a document you told us that you found a curious note on the back of the document. Mr. Prelec, from the document -- I mean, the text, not this note on the back but from the original text on the reverse side of the document to the -- on the right-hand side we see all the addressees, all the people this document was addressed to. We do not know if it was sent to them but it was addressed to them. And you identified those, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You will agree that there are at least 60, if I'm correct, addressees who should receive this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there are 12 brigades and then there are independent units, three, and the 4th Battalion of the military police, so it adds up to 16. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where did you find this document, could you tell us? In what binder alongside whose documents? Among the documents of one of the addressees or among the documents of the sender? Sender is obviously only one, there is only one. Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I described yesterday in my direct testimony, this came out of a box of folders and it was in one of those folders and, as I recall, it was surrounded by a number of other documents bearing on the events of 16 April. It would be possible, as with all of these documents, to give you a precise answer since we have maintained our records of precisely where each document came from, and I'm sorry that I, not anticipating this question, did not bring these materials with me. My recollection is that a substantial number of those documents were, in some way, connected with Mr. Cerkez, but I cannot give you a more precise answer at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But would you agree from your description that it was neither a binder nor a folder titled the Viteska Brigade saying the sender or the addressee and so on and so forth, but on the other hand, you did see such binders; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in a folder which did have a description which was similar or identical to the description of a binder. I think that description indicated the Viteska Brigada, and I do have a record of it but I cannot tell you precisely again at this moment, I've seen so many of these. But I can tell you that there was something corresponding to a binder description on the folder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you agree that there were very many different documents in that particular binder, that there were not only the documents of the Vitez Brigade and were not all -- and those documents were not all issued by the same person?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The note that you mentioned yesterday was, and you saw it with your own eyes on the back of that document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please come closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The document itself was not signed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But it does have a filing stamp, doesn't it? Some call it the distribution stamp.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually don't know what this stamp is. I have always assumed that it was some sort of transmission or communication stamp. I can see it can refer to sending and to receipt. Sometimes one or the other was circled. In this case, it appears that "Received" is underlined, but -- well, I suppose you can see that as well as I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. That document is about that. But one should say that this is a document which was found with one of the addressees, that is what the document looks like. And then it shows also the circled word which is "courier," and does it imply that it was delivered by courier, that that was a possibility; we do not know, but that it is quite possible that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a possibility, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And since there is no signature and it was delivered by courier, and from the general appearance of the document, you cannot say, in fact, whether this is an authentic document or a false one. I mean the document itself, and I'm not referring to the back side of it. There is no way that you can tell; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I don't see the connection between the beginning of your question about the signature and the courier and the conclusion. I suppose, in a strict sense, it's true that I cannot say whether this is an authentic document, but only in the sense that that comment could be made of almost any document, not limited to the broad range we've been discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the basis of your assertion, Mr. Kovacic, that it was delivered by courier?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would remind the Court earlier that we have discussed, I guess, in some occasions a so-called Paket or package system of communications the HVO used which is, indeed, kind of radio transmission with -- aided by computers. So obviously, when the document is sent through radio communication, with or without computer doesn't matter, it cannot be signed. But this document is signed by a courier between two offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just wait a moment. Let us see if the witness can confirm that. You hear what Mr. Kovacic is asserting. Can you say whether that's true or not, Mr. Prelec?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that it does appear to have been sent by courier. I would also draw attention to the top line of that box which indicates "HVO CV" which, in my experience, is the communications centre, centar veze, Vitez. The point I am making is a simple one. There is no reason why it could not have been transmitted to one location by electronic means and then hand carried to another location. So the two are not exclusive, but that's not proof that that's exactly the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you really do not know how this actually happened and there are no ways for you to find out and to conclude how this was done by looking at the documents themselves?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, all I could add would be from my direct testimony yesterday other supporting documentation. One could also indicate what appears to be -- or what appears in the position that often times on many documents an address indication appeared. I'm referring to the Viteska Brigada. I don't recall about this document, but many of these were found in the archive in a way that indicated they had been folded over and this was written on the centre of one of the folded panels. But I suppose to answer your question most simply, beyond those partial means, no, I have no way of knowing certainly how it was delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This same document, since we have already established that it was sent to at least 15 addressees, did you find this particular document in any other folder from which it could be seen that one other addressee also received it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall any other example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to the back page of the document. The note that we have seen and that can be found on the back of the page as such is not signed. It is not a handwritten note. It does not contain any signature, any specification of date or place. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The note was actually written in two different handwritings. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're referring to the "Viteska Brigada" and the remainder, yes. The four lines below that appear to me to be in the same hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I agree. So four lines from the back -- from the bottom and the Vitez Brigade, the title, these two portions of the text were not written by the same person. These are two different handwritings. You yourself have observed that, and I guess we can agree on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, wait a minute. This witness is here about the discovery of the documents. Now you're trying to cross-examine him about handwriting. I don't think he's a handwriting expert. It's not a matter for him. It's a matter for us. If you want to address us on that, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Your Honour. However, the witness has presented this note as being part of a whole. As a layperson, I think he can differentiate between two different handwritings because he has seen the original which was written in two different pencils. Of course I'm not asking for his opinion as an expert in this matter, but I do believe that we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He can be asked whether, as far as he saw, two different pencils were used. He can be asked that because that's a question of fact which he might be able to have observed or not. Mr. Prelec, let me ask you. Can you assist us as to whether two different pencils were used or not? If you can't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether it was pencil, pen, aside from the notes below I'm certain -- I recall as being pencil. But, no, I can't. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, so you don't know nor is there anything on which you can base your conclusions by looking at the document who, when, and where wrote this particular note; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, let me ask you just one more question in relation to this matter. Have you seen any other documents in this huge amount of papers in the archives containing a note here and there written by someone on the back page of a document?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prelec, while inspecting these documents, you didn't come across anything which would be called an operations diary of the Vitez Brigade or a similar type of document which would contain description of operations like the document that you found and that you told us about - I forgot its number - is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Likewise, Mr. Prelec, you have never come across, as far as the Vitez Brigade is concerned, a logbook or an index of issued and received documents such as the one that you found for the Operational Zone, at least for one particular period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, so it was not possible for you to have a random look at the documents or make a random check of the documents that you found in a kind of logbook or an index so that you can see whether the two correspond; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in a logbook, no. There was another way to do this that might assist you. It was the practice, or appeared to be the practice of many subordinate commanders, including Mr. Cerkez, to reproduce the substance of orders received in orders sent out, simply changing, "I order the brigade," to "I order the battalion," and the like. And I saw a great many of these. This is, I suppose, somewhat different from what you're asking. There was no logbook I could consult, or at least, I found no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you were not able to check the sequence of numbers on the documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not able to check the particular number. They -- yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, did you have an opportunity to conduct any technical examination using specific means that exist today to check the date of the document, the type of the document, and so on? Or, rather, let me put it this way: Is it the case that the only method that you used was actually a visual inspection carried out by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like document Z591 to be shown to the witness, please. Mr. Prelec, I'm now going to show you a document that has been admitted into evidence in this case and I should like to ask you whether you have seen this document in one of the folders of the Vitez Brigade. Does it remind you of anything? Have you seen this document, and what is it that you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not this one since it has a line in Dutch, or what appears to be Dutch, at the top and I would have recognised that. I did see lists of names of detained persons but, once again, I've seen so many of these that I would be reluctant to say that I have or have not seen this precise one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For the record, you said that you saw lists of names; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking of such lists, have you ever seen, in connection with them, any marking on the folder or the binder containing an indication of the group or the institution, an institution or a commission for exchanges? Have you seen any such document or any such folder?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see such documents. I don't recall an entire binder, but numbers of such documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, then, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document can be taken back; we are not going to use it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, you mentioned that you have had a number of opportunities to speak with Dr. Kolanovic, the head of the archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From those conversations, or perhaps from some other source, did you come to learn that Croatia has a law on archives that is applicable?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from another source, and I was in no way surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During those conversations, you told us about the problems that you discussed with the relevant authorities, but did you ever hear about a specific legal problem concerning the publication and access of the documents that had been handed over to the archives? As a historian, I'm sure you're aware that there are certain standards that are applied everywhere in this particular field. Has this issue ever cropped up? Has it been discussed and where?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was reported in the media in the Croatian parliament about this question. My impression was that it concerned principally the materials in the custody of the president of the Republic, and there had been a proposal to subject those materials to a classification procedure that would have kept them sealed for, I think, about 25 years. But that proposal did not pass. I am familiar with similar legislation. It's quite common in various countries for various kinds of documents. The materials now in the Croatian State Archive, this is the HVO materials, are, as I said, available by permission of the government to representatives of the defence and of the Office of the Prosecutor and, to my knowledge, no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At any particular point in time, did you or your people at the archive ever receive any formal document issued by the head of the archive whereby these documents are properly classified with their owner being indicated and also indicating their former legal status in accordance with the relevant statutory provisions?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in any way similar. With each batch of copies we got a letter signed by an archival representative and a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor simply confirming that the documents were handed over in English and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Still in relation to this issue, from those conversations that you had and from other contacts that you had with the authorities, were you able to conclude that those documents were, formally speaking, the property of the archive or if they were considered for the property of the institution that was using them, such as HIS or any other similar institution? Were you ever given any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Kolanovic did mention to me once that he, in some ways, regretted receiving this collection because of its enormous size and the amount of work that would go into organising it. And he then said because of international agreements about archival materials, he would have to some day have to give it all to Bosnia. So from his point of view, it would all be for naught. But he did not mention when that would be and I was not able to -- I did not even try to confirm its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that, as far as you are concerned, and perhaps Dr. Kolanovic as well, that in view of the relevant legal provisions, the formal category and the formal status of those documents was not clear.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've said all I know about their legal status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, you said last night that you would be 20 minutes. You have now been three-quarters of an hour. We have a great deal to do this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really sorry. It took a little bit longer than I predicted, but I'm quite certain I have only two or three short questions left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At one point during the examination-in-chief you mentioned some photographs, some pictures that you saw as being part of some documentation that you found at specific locations. Let me be -- let me clarify. On those photographs, one could see boxes but not documents themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think you will also agree with me that from those photographs you were not able to see what those boxes actually contained?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were all filled, or the great majority were filled with binders. That was visible. But if you're asking about what was in the binders, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of the number of binders, you couldn't even tell whether they were empty or full; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me be quite frank: I will put to you that both those boxes were actually planted, that they were not real boxes.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you at least agree with me that that is a possibility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us try and understand what it is you're putting. Now, could you put the question again so we can follow it, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the photographs containing boxes, are you able to claim with certainty that those boxes contained, at least in one part, the documents which you subsequently saw in Zagreb? Just a yes/no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me draw your attention once again to the document we used yesterday, Z2834.2, the letter from the Ministry of Defence sent to Major Radic to the government of the Republic of Croatia. I don't think we need to see the document. Mention was made in that document that by the time the letter was written on the 9th of November, 2000, the Croatian State Archive had managed to collect 3.289 binders, and approximately a 120-metre long file of documents. Another mention was made of 4 kilometres of documents. Is that correct as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that? Could you give us any piece of information about that? What can you say about this huge difference, 3.99 kilometres? Do you have any idea about that? Have you received any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4 kilometre reference was not made to me personally. It was made to another officer of the OTP. That would be the total. It was presented as the total from all sources, and Major Radic, in her letter, is clearly referring to material coming in several shipments from the Ministry of Defence if not one particular part of that Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I've come to my last two questions. Mr. Prelec, as an investigator or an analyst or an historian working for the Office of the Prosecutor, did you ever hold in your hands, did you ever inspect any other document outside of these two groups of documents in Samobor and in the state archive? Did you have documents from any other source except for the documents that are here at the Tribunal with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, unless you consider things that are available to the public. If you're asking did I examine, as in my professional capacity, documents neither from the HVO archive, other archives, in the presidential archive, or our own material presented to me here, I can't think of another -- another case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have never seen any other archive in Zagreb or perhaps in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did obtain documents in Bosnia, but I would not describe it as from an archive. They were from a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So as regards what we discussed about Zagreb and the major part of your investigation or the focus of your investigation, in view of that, we can say that you only had an opportunity to see the documents which Croatian intelligence services had handed over to the state archive, not documents from any other source; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the materials in the HVO archive, to my understanding, do come only from -- from materials in the custody of Croatia. But I did see materials from other sources in the course of my work here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you were aware, and this is what you testified about, that the documents had come from HIS to the state archive, the documents that you inspected, and also from the Ministry of Defence? You don't know of any other third source which would provide the documents to the archive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know a third source, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further -- I'm sorry. I apologise. Just one more question. I had made a brief note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, there were quite a few documents, at least, we received them and you mentioned them, which looked like printouts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Many of such documents, or rather, the majority of those documents were not signed at all?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think you will agree with me if I say that there is no way for you to tell whether they were simple draft documents printed out or final documents, final versions of documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the context in which they were found would be useful in that respect. Things like the document you presented to me earlier is, I think, a good example. Things like a transmission stamp or a courier note or something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have seen quite a few printouts, and those documents, as we have seen, do not have signatures or stamps. So you will agree with me that we cannot say, in respect of those documents, when and where they were issued, whether they were signed or not, and which office they emanated from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there's no stamp, no signature, if it's simply a bare document, the only piece of information I could use at that point would be its location. And one would have to give that a certain amount of weight, but I can't say how much weight. By location, I mean if it's found with a lot of other material from a certain person or if it's found with a sender, then that would suggest it might be a draft. If it's found with the recipient, it would seem unlikely that it's a draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, Dr. Prelec, as a professional, you wouldn't use such a document as a basis for your doctoral thesis, for example, as such?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not go on with this. It really is a pointless question. Yes, now anything more, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm done, Your Honours. Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two areas of inquiry only.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, you were asked by counsel for Kordic yesterday, and I'm going to give you a chance to give a further -- expand your answer. You were asked at page 72, "Q You can't tell in fact, sir, that this is indeed the so-called HVO archive, can you? A I'm certain it is. I don't know on what degree of detail you'd like me to pursue that." Can you expand, please, and provide to the Chamber the basis of your statement that you are certain that it is the so-called HVO archive?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are a variety of reasons, and I suppose the most persuasive one, to me, is the sheer impossibility of it -- of imagining that it would be something else. And I refer to the archive as a whole, not to each individual part of it. It would be like -- I mean, to create something like this would require basically having another war. I mean, we're talking about an astonishing quantity of material which is also, furthermore, interconnected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that many of the documents that I saw were documents that requested some kind of response or action and often that response or action could be found. So, you know, often one could trace an order through three or four different command levels in three or four different parts of the archive that were removed one from another, separated in space. One could also find documents that bore on the same event in generally consistent terms with the kinds of differences that, to me, are familiar from simply having different observers addressing an intense experience like a war. Many of these were small details. There's a principle that I was taught that one could sometimes put greater emphasis on unintended information that, you know -- for example, in one of these documents, the accidental material, so to speak, can be quite revealing. Okay. And this fits together through the course -- I mean, I was down there for three months about, you know. I've read many thousands of these, and it's difficult on this occasion to, you know, come up with specific examples other than the ones I cited, the sort of chains of orders and responses to orders and different references to the same event or to the same kinds of phenomenon. Again, one finds in widely separated areas the general kinds of problems cropping up. Things like petty crime or people leaving their post. I suppose -- I don't know how much longer you want me to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. When you -- again, when you had your interactions directly with the director of HIS, Dr. Zunec, Dr. Zunec referred to this and called this the HVO archive, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was never any doubt about this through any segment of the Croatian government I was ever acquainted with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me move on, Mr. Prelec. The only other inquiry I wanted to ask you to come back to is another question that was put to you by Mr. Sayers was he told you that you were taught -- this is at page 63 and 64 of the transcript. "Q You were taught in your profession, I think, as you say, to assess documents critically and not merely to accept what they say on face value, right? A That's correct." And Mr. Sayers says, "Q To quote a composer from our country, George Gershwin, 'The things you read in the Bible ain't necessarily so.'" What I want to ask you, sir, have you had occasion to look at some of the documents collected with a critical eye, as Mr. Sayers describes, and come to any conclusions about, in fact, are those documents, as he said, internally and externally consistent?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection to the question, Your Honour. That intrudes into the subjects covered by paragraph 15 of the witness' testimony, and I believe that that subject is a question for Your Honours and not for a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it has nothing to do with paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The witness can answer as to whether there was an internal consistency. That was a matter of observation, not a matter of finding of fact which we have to make in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it in light of that exchange, Mr. Prelec. Did you have occasion to examine particular documents, and based upon your observations of that document and how it may have related -- connected to similar documents which you also personally observed or saw, can you tell the Court and give the Chamber, if you can, any example of documents, if you recall, of seeing documents that were again internally and externally consistent?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really almost any document. The internal consistency is, I suppose, more an absence of inconsistency. And I can say the document, and I'm sorry to dwell on this since we went over it so exhaustively yesterday, the 15th of April document leapt out at me. Or it didn't leap out at me but it interested me, having been asked about it, because it was one of these -- basically the only case I can think of in which there was -- or one of an extraordinarily few cases, I'm cautious about saying "only," in which there appeared to be something questionable about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is the one about -- just so we're clear, this is the one about the date on the document and when it was actually issued.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't think of another example. In some investigative files, I believe they were of the security service, but they were -- they concerned, again, cases of ordinary crime. There were numerous references to other documents cited as evidence, much like our own internal documents here would cite other documents as evidence, and those documents did appear. They did broadly support the allegations made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- let me direct your attention to one particular document in closing. Do you recall having looked at a document describing the concerns of the four of the HVO presidents from Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is beyond the scope of direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's one example. It's one specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, how is this relevant to cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's exactly the point that Mr. Sayers raised at page 63 and 64 of the transcript about the examination of particular documents, that you can't -- in looking at a document, he says -- he said specifically the testing of these documents to ensure that they're internally consistent and externally consistent with information. And I've asked the witness about that, and I'm citing this particular document as an example to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- to illustrate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think it's a potentially important document, Your Honour, and I do know that it's one that this witness has -- is familiar with, and I cite it as one example to make a generalisation more consistent. I think the witness can assist the Chamber in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sayers ask about this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That specific document? I don't -- probably not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He didn't suggest that there was something wrong with it and in terms of inconsistency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Nor has he agreed to the document or its admission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shan't allow the question. It did not arise in -- it does not arise out of cross-examination, in our view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me finish with this then, Your Honour, without reference to the particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Prelec, to follow up on counsel's suggestion, in reviewing a number of documents, can you just say this: Did you undertake, on occasion, to in fact examine documents again for their internal and external consistency? Did you do that, and generally, if you can tell the Chamber what was the -- what observations did you make, having done that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions, yes. I -- in terms of internal consistency, meaning was there anything within the document itself that suggested something fishy, to be colloquial, I can't think of another case other than the 15th of April one. It's not impossible that there was, but I can't recall any such case now in any way. In terms of external consistency, one particular document I looked into which was fairly lengthy and presented an extended narrative of events --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is precisely the point. This is Exhibit 1367.1, I believe, a statement by Mr. Vidak and a document that that witness statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: These are matters which we are going to have to discuss in a moment, and I think we've gone far enough. Now, is there anything else, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Not in the time allowed. We would address 673.7, but because of time, we won't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec, could you tell us generally what was the methodology used to test external inconsistencies?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It was very simple. I simply considered the -- well, the assertions and other factual information that could be drawn from the document, and I attempted to make a search or I made a search of other information, other documents that I was aware of that bore on those assertions and facts. This is a long process. Not very long, but it's something that's done with difficulty. It would be done with difficulty for the number of documents that I've read. Generally, one comes up with small differences, and as an historian, small differences don't bother me because there are many explanations for them. What becomes troubling is if they fall into a pattern which suggests a reason to question the overall validity or authenticity of the document, and I have not found anything like that, even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRELEC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prelec. That concludes your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now we turn generally to the exhibits. We have, of course, had the opportunity of looking at the various schedules of exhibits. What we propose is that the first matter on which we would wish to be addressed is the test to be applied in the admission of these exhibits. Once we've considered submissions on this, we will decide on the test. Then having done that, so everybody knows what the test is, we'll start going through the documents. Mr. Scott, I think it's probably for you to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Your Honour, may it please the Court, the position of the Prosecutor's Office on the admissibility of these documents is that these documents should be viewed and treated in substantial measure consistent with the way in which all or virtually all of the other documentary evidence in this case has been treated and received. Further, we would have to submit, Your Honour, that if those rules have changed since the trial started, then we would ask and seek some additional opportunity to meet whatever requirements the Chamber might have. The approach has been to select, through a huge number of documents found in Zagreb, documents that we thought would be most helpful to the Chamber on the issues in this case. As I mentioned yesterday, obviously I can appreciate the fact that it appears to the Chamber and its staff that this is a large volume of material, and again, Your Honour, it depends on one's perspective. It is, in fact, substantially something far less than 1 per cent of the material that's been reviewed. The rules of this Tribunal in terms of evidence are -- I would think it's fair to say at this point in its history, the evidentiary philosophy is one of inclusion rather than exclusion; that this is a Tribunal of professional Judges, that many of the more technical rules of evidence that may apply in some systems and especially the kind of evidentiary issues that come to bear in systems heavily involving lay jurors, that those kind of considerations are not appropriate for this Tribunal and for this Chamber. As has been said many times in the course of this trial, this Chamber is composed of professional Judges familiar with the work of judging and able to look at the totality of the evidence, not one -- and I would suggest and I would ask the Court, not one -- any one item of evidence, be it testimony or document, in isolation but look to the body of evidence and determine what weight to give any particular aspect of it. I would ask the Chamber to be mindful that, as with so many other aspects of the work of this Tribunal, this is not like a national court. It is not like a national police system. Many of the tools that we take for granted in those systems, if you will, the ability to produce custodians of evidence, the ability to produce, for instance, a business records witness, simply either can't be done here or can only be done in some instances with tremendous difficulty, or the evidence is in the hands of hostile parties, parties who have not only not produced evidence but have, in fact, obstructed this Tribunal for years. It puts the Prosecutor in a -- frankly, and the Tribunal really, ultimately the Tribunal as a whole to carry out its mission, it puts us in a very difficult situation if the technical -- types of technical authentication and foundation requirements are required when the only witness who could possibly do those things would be, in this instance, former senior HVO officers, Bosnian -- high Bosnian Croat officials who are hostile, frankly, to this Tribunal and to this case and to the Prosecution. And the Chamber has seen, even in recent days, the difficulty of getting these witnesses to come to court, even when subpoenaed. They evade service or they refuse to come. This is directly -- now, the Chamber, I realise, in the interest of time, is asking -- may ask itself if this is directly connected to the question that the Court has posed. It is directly related because, in applying the test and in determining the appropriate test for this institution, not some other institution, not a court sitting in London or Dallas or Jamaica or elsewhere, this institution, given the difficulties that this body has to deal with. And time after time in its various documents, in its annual reports, in the decisions coming out of both the Trial and the Appeals Chambers, there is the recognition that this is not like a national system and there are unique aspects and unique problems of gathering and presenting evidence in this environment. In fact, in the Kovacevic appeals decision, in a separate decision by Judge Shahabuddeen at pages 4 and 5, he -- His Honour said that the Tribunal has recognised that the application of principles of law to war crimes Prosecution "has to take account of the peculiarities and difficulties of unearthing and assembling material for war crimes prosecutions conducted in relation to the territories of the former Yugoslavia." Judge Shahabuddeen went on to say, "The resulting need for reasonable judicial flexibility is apparent." I believe it is also Judge Shahabuddeen who has stated on other occasions in decisions before the Tribunal that, frankly, in comparison to the work of this Tribunal, the work of the Nuremberg and Tokyo tribunals, relatively speaking, in his terms, not mine, was easy. There was a vast array of material possessed by the occupying forces, former records of the German government, former records of the Tokyo government, which form the basis virtually of all the documentary evidence presented in those cases. And in fact, it was one of the more interesting things, and we've mentioned this at page 5 of the submission we made yesterday, that in looking at the Nuremberg trials, the clearest example is that, that in the international military Tribunal, it was captured German documents which constituted the principal evidence used in those cases. The documents were substantiated by affidavits explaining how they had been captured and safeguarded. It came to be referred to as the Coogan affidavit. They were admitted by the trial court on the basis of their probative value, applying Article 7 of Ordinance number 7 related to the military tribunals, which is very similar to this Tribunal's own rules. And that rule said: "The tribunals shall not be bound by technical rules of evidence. They shall adopt and apply to the greatest possible extent expeditious and non-technical procedure and shall admit any evidence which they deem to have probative value. No requirement of calling a live witness in order to lay a foundation of a document was imposed on the prosecution in the Nuremberg trials." We state in our papers for some pages some of the comparative law from a number of systems, including England and Wales, including Belgium, including France, including a number of systems, about the admission of documentary evidence. I think I could accurately summarise that by saying it is not a high standard. These are some indicia that the document is what it purports to be. It's a separate question from its ultimate relevance. It's simply the question of authentication. Is there some reason to believe that the document is what it purports to be? The document can -- let me add to the Court to say that a document can be absolutely authentic and its content absolutely false, and, therefore, it could be extremely relevant to the Chamber. There could be a document which there is no doubt about its authenticity. For instance, an Ahmici report written by Anto Sliskovic, a person who some would say was up to his eyeballs in the crimes committed in Ahmici. He may have written a report. It may be absolutely authentic. There may be no question that it's his report, his signature, his work, and yet the content of that report may be absolutely false. In fact, a deliberately false cover-up and concealment of crime. The question of authenticity is a specific issue. I submit to the Chamber that, even in national systems, it is not a high standard. It need not be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. It is simply a flexible and practical approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, do you say that we should take no notice of the stage of the trial at which you are seeking to admit this evidence? Because the position is this: That this is evidence, Prosecution evidence, which you're seeking to adduce after the close of the Defence case. Now, you say that the normal rules should apply. Well, of course, that is generally right if this evidence was to be sought to be admitted during the course of your own case. Then those rules would apply. But unless you say we should take no notice of the timing of this, we have, do we not, to take account of where we are in the trial, the effect on the trial of the admission of this evidence, and the question of fairness both to the Prosecution and to the accused? Now, those are all matters which the Trial Chamber has to take account of. It's 11.00 now and if you'd like to think about your submissions, you can give us them at half past 11.00. But we would like to hear them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Mr. President, let me answer the Court's question this way, and I'd like to put it in two parts, and let me forecast, let me preview that I hope that the Chamber will find the second part perhaps -- how do I say it -- more to its liking than the first part. But I must state it in two parts, if the Chamber will allow. Our first position, Your Honours, I think from an institutional perspective and from a legal perspective, the answer to the Court's question has to be: The tests are the same. The tests are the same now as they would be at any point in the trial. We do not have one set of rules of evidence for different parts of the trial; the rules of authentication, the rules of foundation, the rules of witness presentation. Those rules stay the same at all parts of the trial and, of course, they don't change. Secondly, the case was, as the Chamber knows, was intentionally recognising these -- the problems with receiving the evidence from Croatia, a problem with which this Chamber is well familiar. The Chamber has issued binding orders, the Chamber has heard in the midst of various hearings the problems with these issues dating back to this Chamber being constituted and coming on the case. These have not been new issues. Recognising that problem, the Prosecution, in March, when it rested, specifically reserved this part of the case. I have the transcripts here, but I know the Chamber has recognised that before and I won't belabour it, except that this is not something new or surprising. It was forecast back in March of this year that, indeed, with any luck, if I can put it that way -- well, not really luck; as a result of tremendous hard work on behalf of a lot of people, the evidence might become available to the Chamber, it would be submitted. And we have attempted to do that. We have, in fact, been utterly diligent. Again, the point I just made: We have devoted incredible resources and efforts at every level of the OTP in getting this information before the Chamber. The Prosecutor herself has travelled to Zagreb. Tremendous efforts have been made to bring this evidence before the Chamber. Another reason the tests should be the same, and again, Your Honour, in the first part of my answer, is that certainly, if there is to be some consideration given, certainly it would be wrong, we submit, to penalise or prejudice the Prosecution. It's not the Prosecution here that's done anything wrong. We have not done anything wrong except to try to bring this evidence before the Chamber. Sometimes even in international jurisdictions where there is, for instance, Prosecutorial misconduct or police misconduct, there is times when that side of the house, if I may say so, perhaps has to be penalised because of some misconduct. Your Honours, there has not been a hint, not a hint, and even, I must say, for sometimes some quite vociferous opposition from my friends across the courtroom, it has been -- this has been a hard-fought fight. But I submit, Your Honours, if I have heard correctly, I have not heard a hint of a suggestion of misconduct or unethical behaviour in attempting to bring this material before the Chamber. There is, of course, the issue that -- and the flip side of that issue -- excuse me, Your Honours, not only we submit should the Prosecution not be penalised for not having done anything wrong, but we ask the Chamber please to be cognizant of this. Don't reward the obstructors. If there is someone to be penalised here in some form, and that's probably -- we can't resolve this issue today, that has been historically, and even recently, the State of Croatia. But I ask the Chamber, the Prosecution asks the Chamber, don't penalise the Prosecution case because of the years of obstruction of the Tudjman regime. Don't reward them by obstructing and excluding evidence now that this Tribunal should have had years ago. And without being offending or abrasive to the Court, I have to be firm on this point: To exclude evidence now would do exactly that. It would say to the dark forces, it would say to the dark and evil forces that have obstructed this Tribunal for years, "You won. You've kept this evidence out of the Chamber's hands for so long that the time came at the end of the case when it was finally available and it was excluded." That is, I submit, the wrong message for this institution, not only in this case but in another cases, to be sending to the former states of Yugoslavia, or in the next Tribunal some other state, to send the message, "You can successfully obstruct. If you hold the evidence back long enough, you will succeed and it will never come in. Because at the last minute if some Prosecutor, in the future, succeeds after years of effort to obtain that evidence and it comes in late in a case, don't worry, it will be excluded." That would be the wrong message to send. The Court gave us, the Prosecution, a 30 October deadline --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask you something, Mr. Scott. You have spoken, and you have actually just requested or appealed to the Chamber not to penalise the Office of the Prosecutor, that is, the Prosecution in general, by excluding a number of exhibits. I should like to know, in what way would the Office of the Prosecutor be penalised if the Chamber, as it was said to you at the beginning by holding open this case until now, in what way would the Prosecutor be penalised if the Chamber does not admit into evidence those exhibits which are of a repetitive nature and which merely reinstate the elements that have already been admitted or tendered into evidence by your party if they do not bring anything new, anything particularly new to your case concerning either the culpability or innocence of the accused? In what way would the Prosecutor be penalised?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Bennouna. In that respect, and that gets -- would get to the second part of my answer, if that is what the Chamber has in mind in terms of striking some further balance, for lack of another term. If that's what the Chamber has in mind, then I think we may not be that far apart. If, on the other hand, by the discussion of possible -- of a different test or more rigid standard, it would lead to the larger exclusion of relevant evidence beyond what you've just outlined, Judge Bennouna, then obviously we would have a much greater concern. By I think on the points that you've made, Your Honour, I don't think we're that far apart, and I would come to that further in my second part. Let me just finish with my full answer to the Chamber's question. Before we turn to the second part, let me also just point out we must -- that the Chamber gave us a 30 October deadline. We complied as best we could. Certainly not perfectly, and the Defence has reminded us and undoubtedly will continue to remind us of some imperfections in a -- a particular document wasn't listed or a particular document, unfortunately, didn't come off the Xerox machine the way that it should have. We weren't perfect. Dealing with this much material and this information, I'm sure that everybody in the courtroom can understand that sometimes mistakes are made. But the Chamber gave us a deadline. There was no forecasting at that time of a different standard. We simply marshalled the evidence as best we could. Again, we were very selective and produced this information according to the Court's timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I had no idea that you were to produce 260 documents. If you had told the Chamber months ago that you were going to produce 260 documents, you would have got a reaction. I assumed it was going to be the order of a dozen or something like that, something really important. So the fact that there was no more stringent test indicated was because nothing of this magnitude was anticipated. Because it has been, then we've got to look at it again. And the fact that you have cut material down, that is to your credit, of course, and we accept you've had to work very hard, but it is nothing to the point now. The point now is what should be admitted in this trial at this stage? You cannot continue as though this was the middle of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Effectively, you are trying to bringing in a huge amount of material, and the Chamber has to strike a balance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry. I obviously hear the Chamber and I understand that point. I can't -- I won't even try to, or I certainly won't argue with the Court as to what it expected the number of documents to be. All our expectations might have been different but it's probably not productive to argue that other than I certainly hear the President's point on that. Let me turn to the second part of our answer, then. We have, in fact, as the Chamber just -- as the President just indicated, have, in fact, in our view, yielded a great deal. Had this been -- and I must say we are -- from a legal perspective, in terms of procedurally having reserved our case, we are in our case. We have to go back in time. If all of us -- if this Chamber could step into a time capsule and go back to the Prosecution's case-in-chief and had this evidence been made available on a timely basis, then we certainly would have submitted it and it probably would have been more, frankly. As much as the Chamber might not want to hear that, it might well have been more than 260 documents. But the fact of the matter is we have yielded. We have yielded by being more selective. And again, that may strike the Chamber as odd or different than its view, but I can tell you, the Chamber, that we have been more selective than we otherwise might have been ten months ago. What is yielded, Your Honour, in meeting the test and striking the balance that the President has indicated, what has been yielded, if something must be yielded, in light of the situation, again, Your Honours, certainly shouldn't be yielded at the expense of the Prosecution case other than the type of considerations that Judge Bennouna has pointed out. If it is truly repetitious, if it is truly peripheral -- and we will have to discuss those things because obviously we will have the view that something we have submitted is not, in fact, peripheral -- but broadly speaking, taking Judge Bennouna's considerations in mind, we agree there is room to yield, if yielding to the Chamber is the right word on that point. But beyond that, certainly, Your Honours, we would take the position we should not yield, be required to yield in ways that penalise the Prosecution case again where the Prosecution has done nothing wrong. Secondly, further, we would suggest, Your Honours, that while the President yesterday used the word that this was an extraordinary situation, I don't think it's extraordinary in the sense that sometimes the word "extraordinary" is intended to use "extraordinary" in some suspect or questionable way. It is in some sense unusual. It is unusual for -- again for all the reasons we've discussed and the reasons that bring us to this situation today, for factors and forces, unfortunately, beyond all of our control. We have shown next -- my next point is that we have shown reasonable diligence. I think that there's been no evidence that suggests -- and notwithstanding the cross-examination of Mr. Prelec, there's been no substantial showing of anything less than complete diligence since March of this year to bring this evidence before the Chamber. I think there can be no bona fide question about that, I would submit, Your Honours. There's been a tremendous effort, tremendous expense to bring this evidence before the Chamber as quickly as possible, and I might say the Chamber may please appreciate that, again, this selection of material is again even a smaller selection than the amount brought from Zagreb and -- smaller than the amount disclosed to the Defence. We have disclosed substantially more than this out of our disclosure obligations; in fact, indeed, beyond our disclosure obligations. There was never a Rule 66(B) request for document discovery in the case. There never has been. But we have undertaken, under these particular circumstances, throughout the course of the summer, to provide this material, to disclose this material as it came in and as translated to the Defence. I'm sure, I hope, the Defence would confirm that, over the months, we have served a number of bundles of documents, bundles much bigger than the 260, and some of it being arguably exculpatory. They've had that, and we've taken that big bundle and now even gone to this much. So again, Your Honours, we have been extremely diligent on all sides to bring this evidence before the Chamber. The question of relevance, I think there was something, Mr. President, in your words yesterday about there being -- about reference to the core relevance -- going to core issues and not the peripheral issues in the case. We would agree with that. Don't question that issue again at this particular stage, and again that goes to the point I made a moment ago. In fact, we have been more selective than we otherwise would have been. There are many more documents that talk about Dario Kordic. There are many more documents that talk about events in Central Bosnia. There are many more documents that talk about the Vitez Brigade. And had we been going back in time a year, a year and a half, much more of that evidence might well have been included. But in recognising this very reality, we have already been more selective again, believe it or not; we have been more selective than we otherwise would have been. We would agree that documents that shed substantial new light, or we would urge the Chamber that the documents that shed substantial new or additional light should be admitted and that they are not, in any sense, peripheral, and I will give -- I'm going to give the Chamber some examples of that. Obviously, I know we'll come to particular documents eventually, but let me again speak in broader terms at the moment. For instance, there is now a collection of documents which reveal -- at least to the Prosecution, presumably known to Mr. Kordic from day one, but revealed to the Prosecution only recently, that there was, in fact, an apparent split or division between various of the authorities in Central Bosnia and that there were a number of the HVO presidents in Central Bosnia, including the presidents of the Vitez municipality, the president of the Busovaca municipality, and the Novi Travnik and the Travnik municipalities which, apparently, were in great opposition to Mr. Kordic. The fact that they resented so much his iron hand of control in Central Bosnia speaks volumes about the power that this defendant exercised. It speaks volumes. They resented the fact that this was the man in charge. They chafed at it. They didn't like it. There is document after document that talks about that, and that's not a peripheral issue at all. It goes directly to the power of that defendant. Another area that is not peripheral, obviously -- this one may be more obvious than some of the others but, in any event, I note it -- obviously those documents involving Mr. Kordic giving military orders are clearly exercising military authority. Surely that evidence must be admitted. Surely the Prosecution should not be penalised by that type of evidence being excluded. Documents concerning Serb/Croat cooperation. Of the -- there are some 18 or 20 documents that talk specifically on the issues of the fact that -- in fact in most of -- in most if not all of 1993, certainly the middle of 1993, there was extensive cooperation from the Serb side and the Croat side in Central Bosnia, even to the point of the Serbs, for payment, providing artillery support to the Bosnian Croats. Now, why is that not a peripheral issue? We submit to the Chamber -- the Prosecution submits, Your Honours, that it has been one of the themes of the Defence case that, "We weren't fighting. We weren't so much concerned about the Muslims or we couldn't have been committing war crimes against the Muslims because we were worried about the Serbs and we were sending troops to the confrontation line with the Serbs." In fact, in large measure, in Central Bosnia, not true. The Croats and Serbs were fighting each other in other parts of Bosnia, but not in Central Bosnia, not in 1993, and certainly in the spring and summer of 1993. They were working with each other. They were arranging passage through each other's territory. That's what the documents show. They were paying each other for oil and trading oil and artillery.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me. My apologies to the interpreters. Those documents are not peripheral at all. And finally, as an example, there are documents that, while put into the Zagreb evidence category for the purposes of this week's exercise, proceedings, there are certainly documents in there that have a rebuttal effect that rebut positions taken by the Defence, the two Defences. And certainly those documents, or certainly the Prosecution should not be penalised to have documents that rebut Defence positions to be excluded. That is -- that's a long answer but the two-part answer that I told the Chamber that I would give it. We don't think the Rules of Evidence, in fact, change. We do recognise and acknowledge that there are some realities of play here and that we have tried to be, in fact, quite selective. We have tried, in fact, to talk about core relevance. Subject to further review of documents, according to the lines that Judge Bennouna has suggested, we are prepared to concede that there are some documents around the edges that we can probably cut away, but we may not -- I have to say, it may or may not be, time will tell, but it may not be -- at least, our position would not be that necessarily may not be as small a number as the Chamber might like, but we can, I think -- there's a recognition, we acknowledge, Your Honours, in good faith that we think we can work around the documents to reduce it to a smaller number. Now, let me finish by -- that was a long answer to the Court's very specifically, but let me just, for the purposes of the record on this evidence -- not for the record, for the purposes of persuasion, address a few other points that have been raised in the last few days. The type of documents that have been received are primarily of two types, broadly speaking. If the Court will allow me a second, I'm cutting across my notes because, in the last few minutes, I've probably touched on a number of these issues. If the Court will just bear with me for a moment. The Zagreb evidence, Your Honour, the evidence we've brought before the Chamber is relevant, it is admissible. As I began to say, there are basically two types of documents, two broad categories of documents that have been tendered to the Chamber. HVO documents which this Chamber has been seeing now for the past 18 or 19 months, that accounts for probably 90 per cent of the collection. There is then a small number of documents, I don't know, something around 30 of the ones we've submitted, approximately some 30 arguably are not HVO archive but come otherwise from the State of Croatia. Now, the production of this document by a state, all of these documents were produced by a state pursuant to Article 29 of the Tribunal's Statute. That statute creates an obligation in paragraph 1 of that: "States shall cooperate ... in the investigation and prosecution of persons accused ..." et cetera. Number 2: "States shall comply without undue delay with any request for assistance or an order issued by a Trial Chamber including, but not limited to: ... the taking of testimony and the production of evidence." All of this evidence, in one form or another, has officially been produced to this Tribunal by a UN member state. Now, until the defence, not by allegations but by some affirmative act of evidence, by some affirmative showing, indicates why the production of documents by a UN member state shall be taken as less than reliable, that they are not what they purport to be. They are not authentic. They are not the HVO archive that HIS has possessed for a number of years in which the director of HIS, Dr. Ozren Zunec, said, "This is HVO archive." In the absence of contrary evidence -- evidence, not allegations -- the production of that material by UN member state should be taken as authentication. As to the non-HVO documents, the very small number that are our other documents, those are documents have the state -- from the records of the state of Croatia. And there's been much bandied about -- if I can put it that way -- about the HIS and SIS documents. These are the official records, or many of them come from the official records of the Bosnian Croat intelligence agency. They weren't fabricated certainly by the Prosecution. These are documents that were produced to this Tribunal pursuant to binding orders or pursuant to Article 29 requests for assistance by UN member states. Those are documents provided to this Tribunal for the purposes of this case.
