If the Kordic or Cerkez Defence suggests that there is some additional authentication beyond that that's required, we would be prepared and, again, in ex parte session, in closed session, Your Honours, as we suggested yesterday, and I know time is incredibly important to the Chamber, but I think at some time before this exercise is completed it may be necessary to make this record, we would be prepared to tell the Chamber the tremendous steps that have been taken to bring additional -- even additional and more evidence before the Chamber in terms of authentic -- more specific background information and authentication on these documents. Suffice it to say for these purposes, in the time allowed and in a public forum, we have done everything possible to bring that information to the Chamber. Some weeks ago - it's been already reported in the Croatian press so I'm not saying anything that's not already in the public domain - summonses were served for a number of these officials in Croatia, the names of many of whom you have heard in the last two days, to come and talk to us and tell us about these documents, and the State of Croatia did not serve a single summons. Not a single person appeared to be interviewed. We asked the State of Croatia to provide a written report of the HVO archive, how the Republic of Croatia came to possess the archive and give us the full history. And they did produce finally last week -- they did produce two reports, two of which the Chamber saw yesterday. In fact, Judge Robinson asked me about one of them, and I agree it doesn't have much identifying information on it, but that's how the State of Croatia produced it to us, to explain, as limited as it is, as imperfect as it probably is, the history of these documents, or at least some of these documents. We asked for the State of Croatia to designate a responsible senior official to come before this Chamber and authenticate this material, to come and sit here and tell the Chamber about it. They did not do so. So I want so say that now for these purposes to say, Your Honour, it isn't for lack of trying. We have tried to bring further detailed information about these documents before the Chamber and the results have been as I've outlined them. Let me just again cut -- see where we -- obviously the Chamber must be or should be guided by the Appeals Chamber decision, in fact, in this very case on an interlocutory appeal, about one of the so-called HIS documents. And the Appeals Chamber came back and said that "The impugned decision of the Trial Chamber is consistent with the settled law of the International Tribunal, that there is no legal basis for the applicant's," and this is the Kordic Defence, "... there is no legal basis for the applicant's argument that the proof of authenticity is a separate threshold requirement for the admissibility of documentary evidence." We certainly -- that is certainly our position. It certainly would be the law, in any event, having been stated by the Appeals Chamber. And in considering the body of the Zagreb evidence, there should not be, if you will, a double standard but the proof of authenticity goes to the overall consideration of the evidence by the Chamber in assessing its authenticity and determining the weight that the Chamber ultimately would give it. We would -- there are other points, Your Honour, in the interests of time -- the Defence in one of their filings yesterday made several arguments, most of which have been addressed in one fashion or another. They said, for instance, that, well, some of these documents couldn't be from the archive because they didn't have the archival stamp. I think the Chamber is aware of that situation at this point. There's some suggestion -- there has been some suggestion in the Kordic brief that somehow when the door to the archive was first opened to the Prosecution in May of this year, that somehow we would have instantaneous, of course, access and knowledge of the whole collection and that, therefore, we've been less than diligent because -- well, if we've had the whole collection in May, why is it only being presented only by the 30 October schedule of this Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, really - I believe at least I speak only in my own name - I think that the way you're presenting your argument is somewhat abusive. Even before we returned, we received your document in writing with all the argumentation in writing, and that includes reference to other documents, different dates, and so on and so forth. Do you think it natural that, after all this now, you can take the floor too now for perhaps more than half an hour we have to listen to you in spite of all the information you have given to us in writing? I do not think there exists a single court in the world which would allow this. That is, not only do we have a document in writing but then also argumentation which is highly repetitive and more than repetitive of what has already been said in writing. One needs to bear in mind the patience of the Chamber and the time which you were allotted to present your arguments. I'm sorry to have to say this to you, but you should bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. You need not be reluctant about saying it. These are important issues. Obviously, this evidence is very important to all sides and to the Chamber. While I can assure the Chamber that I have two or three more comments and will bear, Judge Bennouna, your comments in mind and even limiting it further, let me just say -- if the Chamber will allow me, let me just say that the time devoted to this issue so far is excessive given the magnitude of the issues involved. This is, in fact, coming to the end of this trial and concerning some evidence that this Tribunal has been seeking for a long time. But I understand your points, Judge Bennouna, and I will make a couple of quick points and sit down. It does have to be said that there are -- sometimes it appears to be the attempt to suggest that it's -- it's only the Prosecution that has burdened, if that's the term, the Chamber, these proceedings with documents. That is certainly not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we don't need argument about that. We can see what the Defence have produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's in terms of the binders. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. And on a smaller point on that, in fact, the defendants to date have tendered a number of documents from so-called Zagreb evidence, a substantial volume, without questioning -- apparently questioning or raising issues about their authenticity or value. They have -- both Defence teams have put in substantial amounts of Zagreb documents. We think that the Chamber must, again, be -- take into consideration, when it comes to consider the evidence, that it is, as Mr. Prelec said, it is the way that the documents fit together and tell a picture as a whole. And when the Chamber comes to the point of exercising its discretion on individual exhibits, we would ask the Chamber to bear in mind that a document which may appear on its face in isolation to be peripheral may not be peripheral at all. It may indeed, for instance, be one of the very documents that again, as an example, Mr. Prelec says when you take that document and consider it in light of another document, you see that both of them are reinforced, both of them each corroborating the other. In some sense, the weight -- the body of this -- this body of evidence has to be viewed, we submit, largely as a whole. If the Court will just give me a moment, I'll see if there's other comments, and I'll be complete. Your Honours, that concludes my comments. I do appreciate the Court's patience sincerely for being able to lay these issues -- important issues before the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I say that I agree wholeheartedly with the comments made by Judge Bennouna. And this is not just in relation to you, Mr. Scott, I think for the Defence as well. One of the practices I see as developing in the Tribunal and which I think is positive is a system in which parties present briefs so that when they come into court, they need not address the Court at length. I think in light of the brief that you presented, a presentation of 10 or 15 minutes would have been entirely appropriate. Mr. Sayers may take a hint from that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, our position is as stated on pages 1 to 8 of our brief -- 1 to 7, actually. I believe the question that the Presiding Judge posed was what standards would have to apply, and I think that we've fairly set out the law of this Tribunal, not of other jurisdictions, in those pages. But with the Trial Chamber's permission, I'd like to spend no more than five minutes just addressing three general points. First, the indictment in this case was confirmed five years ago. There's been a frantic last-minute quality to this Prosecution really since the beginning of this trial in April of last year when disclosures were delayed for unexplained reasons, and that pattern of late disclosure has become consistent and constant in this case. The Court will recall that some suggestion was made by the Prosecution that some of this massive quantity of evidence that has continually deluged us for the last few months serves a rebuttal function. The Court ordered rebuttal exhibits to be filed by October the 30th and about 28 were filed. So that's, I would suggest, a full response to the argument made by the Prosecution on that point. Secondly, the Court was completely unambiguous in ordering these new materials in, we would submit, extraordinary dispensation given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. But the point I was making, Mr. President, was the materials were ordered to be delivered by October the 30th. That's the only point that I was making. With respect to these materials, we have not been privy to the interactions between the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. All of the proceedings against Croatia have been ex parte, so I do not have any observations to make on that other than this: The Prosecution says it shouldn't be penalised by the actions of the Republic of Croatia. Mr. Kordic respectfully suggests that he should not be penalised either. In fact, the Tribunal's jurisprudence in the September 2000 decision of the Appeals Chamber makes it perfectly clear that the protection of the rights of the accused is paramount in criminal proceedings. Two final points, Mr. President. First, the general concern articulated by the Trial Chamber, we would submit, is perfectly appropriate. We've closed our case. Now the Prosecution seeks to have another case against us. That, I think, is unfair and it raises fundamental and important Article 21 concerns. We have put our position in previous paper on that point and I won't repeat it. Second, particular concerns are raised by some of the evidence that has been raised, and we've articulated our position with respect to that in our brief, most particularly the anonymously-authored documents assertedly emanating from various intelligence organs and spying agencies. No authentication has been laid for those. Some argument could be made that no authentication is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While you're on the point, yes. I mean, Mr. Scott points out that this issue, this very issue has been in front of the Appeals Chamber when you appealed the admissibility of one of these documents, and you've heard what the result was. We've been reminded of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just pause. That being so, if the issue arose during the course of the evidence in chief, it would be -- or the Prosecution case, rather, it would be difficult for you to argue that the document -- a similar document should not be admitted. Now, what is the difference now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The difference was, Mr. President, that our objection was based principally upon a requirement for authentication, a requirement for some knowledgeable witness to come before the Court and say, "Yes, this is indeed what it purports to be." And you're quite right; the Appeals Chamber has said there is no such requirement in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, but there is a requirement for reliability, Mr. President. We've set that out on page 2 of our brief in the Tadic hearsay decision. It's been reiterated in the Delalic decision that's examined on page 3 of our brief, and most recently it's been very vigorously applied in the July the 21st, 2000 decision reversing the Trial Chamber's admission of the (redacted) exhibit. Reliability, that's the key. And documents, in order to be admissible, have to have some component of reliability, and that's why we have requested the Trial Chamber to exclude Exhibit Z1380.4 and Z1406.1 for the reasons stated in our brief. And I won't repeat them other than to say this: The Prosecution was permitted to use those exhibits to cross-examine particular defence witnesses on particular propositions contained in those documents, and the propositions put to the witnesses were absolutely refuted and there is no other evidence in the record to support them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, therefore, you can say or it can be said that you've had the opportunity or the opportunity has been given to the Defence to rebut the allegations that are made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One could say that, Mr. President, but the point I'm making is paragraph 18 of the Tadic decision, it's quite unequivocal on the issue and I think articulates a perfectly reasonable and sensible rule which says Sub-rule 89(D) provides further protection against prejudice to the Defence for, if the evidence has been admitted as relevant and having probative value, it may later be excluded if it is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. And here, Mr. President, it is. The anonymous authors of these documents, we have no idea who they are. We have no idea the sources upon which their conclusions and conjectures are based, as we've said. We have no way to confront the author, no way to confront the sources of the information, and I think we've accurately summarised the evidence adduced so far which contradicts every single factual assertion, or most of the factual assertions contained in these anonymous documents, certainly insofar as Exhibit Z1380.4 and 1406.2 are concerned. There is no support for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, do you know how many of the documents fall into that category, the anonymous ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I have not counted them because of the most recent disclosures, and I really don't know whether there are any in there, but before the materials that we received on Saturday afternoon, Your Honour, I think there are approximately 20 or 30 of the intelligence agency reports that are the subject of our brief. Now, with respect to the general rules that are articulated by the Prosecution, Mr. President, those are, as you've indicated, the general rules. They apply generally. But we're not at the point in this case where those general rules which we all know have particular application. The -- we've closed our case, and the Prosecution's closed its case. Let me just finish on this particular issue. This is not a new issue in this case where the very thinnest of evidence from anonymous sources is considered for admission. We've been here once before. Let me just remind the Trial Chamber that on May 10th, 1999 during the examination, direct examination of Dr. Mujezinovic, some effort was made to have Dr. Mujezinovic say that he'd heard from a person by the name of Trpimir Vujica that supposedly he'd seen an order that required Dr. Mujezinovic to be put to death. Pretty graphic evidence, but the only evidence of what this fellow Vujica was supposedly going to say. And the Presiding Judge specifically posed the question: "Because the case is difficult to prove, are you saying we should have the thinnest sort of evidence in?" That's page 2.214 of the transcript. And the answer was, effectively, yes. Well, the evidence was excluded and let me just suggest to the Trial Chamber that that was a very wise decision because eight months later, eight months after this evidence had attempted to be adduced, we were given a statement taken by Trpimir Vujica on February 22nd, 2000 and he was asked whether Mr. Kordic had supposedly issued any such order for the killing of Dr. Mujezinovic, whether he'd seen it, and his answer was as follows, "No. That is not correct. I did not tell him so, neither have I seen such an order. In fact, I have not contacted Dario Kordic in my life." That's the kind of situation that we have before us with respect to the anonymous documents. We've been there before. The Court has ruled to exclude that sort of evidence because it's unreliable, and we would respectfully submit to the Court that it should do the same again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall do my best to be very brief indeed. To begin with, I second everything that Mr. Sayers has said and there is no need to go back to that, but perhaps I might point out two or three minor things that were not mentioned so far. First, in the Prosecutor's brief in writing, which is dated 20th November and then in -- under Zagreb documents, item 4, item 4 says that it seems that the Defence, the defendants have also already offered or admitted as many as 200 to 300 Zagreb documents. I could not really check that, but I think that is overstating it and by a long shot. It is also quite true that we did use some of these documents, but only when we were examining witnesses. That is, we used witnesses and, through them, in a very conventional manner, we laid the foundation for those documents. They did not turn up out of the blue. Documents [as interpreted] identify them, or they were about the events they were testifying about. There was the context both in terms of time and place. So evidently, those are certain things which simply do not hold water in this brief. Secondly, in the documents that we received from the Prosecution and which had been narrowed down to the list the Prosecution wishes to introduce, there is at least one example of documents which had already been tendered and used as exhibits in the Blaskic case, such as Z673.4. You will no doubt ask me if there are any such examples, and my answer is that I do not know. I went through our database, the documents which are published, which were disclosed, which are accessible to us, and which we received. Unfortunately, for reasons well-known, we were not given access to documents, to sealed documents in the Blaskic case, which I believe the OTP could see as an organisation. I could see at one of the documents used in the Blaskic case and, of course, one can assume that there are quite a number of such documents. Evidently, we could have been given one of those documents at a time when it would have been proper in such proceedings. I do not insist on the strictest criteria before the opening of the trial, but had we at least been given such a document before we started our case. Then one of the more serious objections of this Defence team is that, amongst the adduced documents, proposed documents, especially the HVO documents found in Croatia, quite a number of them, I do not know how many, I did not count them, but I should say there are no less than 40 documents which were issued by Cerkez himself or officers directly subordinate to him after 31st of September, 1993. In other words, beyond the scope of the indictment. Needless to say, if those were documents in which, for instance, Cerkez was referring to certain things covered by the indictment, I would not be objecting to it. I am only mentioning those documents which have to do only with the current situation, orders such and such action that particular day, and everything is happening after 31st of September. Again, report on a particular event on that particular date or the date before, but again, after the September 31st. Such documents are evidently completely irrelevant and immaterial from the point of view of the temporal scope of the indictment. Even if one looked at it analytically, I do not think that the pretext would hold water when it is said that these documents are being used to demonstrate a particular pattern of behaviour, or at least that is usually not the case when it comes to documents signed by Cerkez or his men which came into existence after 31st of September, 1993. This is merely the example of documents which merely encumber the record and make more difficult the work, not only of the Chamber, but also of the Defence, which has to somehow find its way through this jungle of documents while in point of fact they should have four or five such documents and not more than that. The second objection, which I believe you understood because we asked a number of questions about this, was the fact, and I think this is common knowledge, there is no need to really have to prove it. That is that the document, that the HVO archive which reaches Zagreb by some mysterious routes and ways were, in point of fact, in the possession of at least three intelligence services for not less than six years. It is from the documents that we are getting from this which allow us to doubt, and doubt suffices, that among those intelligence services and then again at a different level between factions within such intelligence services, there are conflicting interests and positions both with regard to the events which were happening on the ground and events -- and things that were happening after the war. So one can realistically assume that there are some forged documents amongst them, and perhaps when it comes to rejoinder, perhaps we shall try to go into it, time permitting. Now, I really do not want to use more of your time than necessary, but I agree with Mr. Sayers and the question is when did we get a particular document at this stage. And in most of the cases, documents for which the foundation has not been laid, we believe that it would be highly prejudicial for the Defence, because at this point in time, the Defence simply has no time to go into certain things intimated by these documents. In a part, my learned friend, Mr. Scott, said, "Do not reward the Defence because the Prosecution was unable to obtain documents from Croatia in time." And I can show you the other side of the coin. Do not punish my client because Croatia has failed to provide documents, because you cannot blame my client for that. I believe that the gist of the thing is the question of the fair trial because this is not whether the Chamber will commend or perhaps reprimand the Prosecution for doing something or not doing something. What we are talking here is the rights of the accused, because it is his rights which are specified in the statute and the accused is entitled to a fair trial. If such documents are allowed at this stage in this trial, and if they are adduced at this stage, I think that the question would then arise of the fairness of the trial to which every accused is entitled. That is laid down and I need not go into that. Just one more thing. At one point, it was said that Croatia has submitted documents. I may be somewhat paranoid, and I do apologise for that but by saying that, an implication is made that a state as an entity has given documents and therefore that state can guarantee the authenticity of such documents. That assertion is not true because Croatia did not give documents. What actually happened was that Croatia told the Prosecutor, "Gentlemen, here you are. Here are the documents which are in the possession of the state at this time concerning your case and your indictment." And we have heard the testimony about that today and we have seen a number of written documents. So it was the OTP that entered the premises of the Croatian Archive and selected the documents that they needed on the basis of a certain criteria and accessibility in general. It was not the State of Croatia that actually looked into those documents and carried out an authentication of the documents which would have been done in accordance with appropriate criteria. The State of Croatia simply told the Prosecutor to do it himself. So we do not have any special guarantee of any state institution, let alone the relevant authorities of the state that those documents are indeed authentic documents. With this, I would like to conclude my submissions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has had the opportunity of considering this matter and, of course, during the break, during argument we have considered it. Having heard the submissions, the test we propose to apply is this: First of all, we bear in mind that the Prosecution did not formally close its case as far as the Zagreb documents were concerned, and so technically, we are within its case. However, that is a technicality, and the reality of the position cannot be ignored, which is that the admission of this evidence is being sought after the close of the Defence case, and that is a consideration which we must have in mind. Accordingly, the test which we will apply is as follows: First, the material must be new in the sense of not having been available to the Prosecution, with due diligence, before the end of its case. Pausing there, I do not understand it to be suggested that any of this material was, in fact, available at that time and, accordingly, it is accepted that it is new. If that is not the case in relation to any material, then the Defence should point it out. Going on with the test, second, the material must not be cumulative, that is, a repetition of evidence already given, and it must be of significant relevance to the core issues in the case, such as those relating to the conduct of the accused. Third, the admission of the evidence must be in the interests of justice, that is, in the interests of assisting the Court in determining the guilt or innocence of the accused and not be contrary to Rule 89(D). That is the test that we will apply. The admissibility of each exhibit will, of course, be considered separately. I would add this: It's been submitted that to exclude the evidence would be to penalise the Prosecution and to reward those who may have obstructed the disclosure of this material. It's also submitted that to admit the evidence would be or may be to penalise the Defence. Whether a party is penalised or not or obstructers are rewarded is not a relevant consideration for the Court. We have to apply the law, we have to try to establish the truth, we have to ensure the fairness of the trial to both parties, and we also have to ensure that this trial is conducted expeditiously, which means, at the present time, that it is concluded expeditiously and in a timely fashion. Those are the considerations which govern the exercise of our discretion. That being so, the time is ten to one. It may be a useful activity to consider what exhibits we have to consider. At least, let's make sure we have everything in front of us. As I understand the position, there are three schedules, entitled "Kordic," Cerkez," and "Miscellaneous."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A completely cumulative and repetitive document, Your Honour. Also, it hardly goes to the issues of core significance in this case which is the guilt or innocence of the accused on the crimes alleged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, clearly the issues in the case involve Mr. Kordic's involvement in the Vares municipality as well including Stupni Do. So it does go directly to that issue of his authority and particularly in that region. The next document is 438.3. I'm sorry, I may have skipped one, 437.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That has apparently been exhibited. Indeed. Yes, I remember that. 437.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then we can go to 438.3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before we go there, Mr. President, I hope the Court will notice Exhibit Z437.1 is another of the genre of documents which is just on a blank page. It's not on any letterhead. It's not signed. It's not stamped. And we have no idea -- and there is no way to tell whether this is just a draft document or a real document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it in, Your Honour? I thought it was already in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Unless I misunderstood, I thought Mr. Sayers got on his feet and raised a question about 437.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's been admitted. He wanted to make some extra point about it, but it's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 438.3. This is again a Kordic order concerning specifically Karacici [phoen] village in February of 1993, purports to be giving orders concerning the entire Operative Zone. Item number 2, for instance, says, "The Operative Zone is to inform UNPROFOR," et cetera. Copied to, among others, Colonel Blaskic. So we submit, Your Honour, that it's Colonel Kordic giving military orders and turning a particular village to the entire Operative Zone and showing his authority, copied to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, completely cumulative and repetitive; secondly, not signed, not stamped, not on letterhead, and, therefore, not useful in determining the guilt or innocence of Mr. Kordic, and we would submit that admitting this document would not be consistent with the interests of ensuring a fair trial under Rule 89(D). In addition, the document, even if it were signed, would have been signed by the President of the HZ HB, Your Honour, and clearly Mr. Kordic was never that. So whoever it was that prepared this document, obviously didn't even know what Mr. Kordic's title was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, in terms of authentication, Your Honour, it bears the Paket communication stamp that's clearly indigenous, if you will, to the document. It also bears a Zagreb archive stamp. So we believe there is no bona fide objection as to its authenticity. The next document is 439.2. There is a series here, Your Honour, together, without breaks, but we'll come back to some breaks. 439.2 is a Blaskic order, and very specifically, Your Honour, the significance of this document is the sentence preceding the word "order" on the first page, where it indicates that Blaskic is giving an order on the basis of an order by Kordic because of the attacks by Muslim forces and, "On the basis of an oral order by Colonel Dario Kordic, I hereby issue the following." So it's important for that reason. It's also an important reason because it shows Colonel Kordic's direct involvement in directing artillery and missile fire. Exactly subject matter of the recording. The recording indicates, around this same time period, the famous, "Let me hear the missile roar," and here we have an order from Kordic to Blaskic on, in fact, a multiple-rocket launcher. So we believe it's highly significant and bears the stamp, the Herceg-Bosna stamp, and a Zagreb archives stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but one thing it doesn't bear is Colonel Blaskic's signature. In the Croatian original, you'll notice that it's signed Za Pukovnik/Blaskic, for Colonel Blaskic. So obviously someone prepared this and apparently, therefore, it must be, at the very least, double hearsay; whoever prepared it receiving an asserted account from Colonel Blaskic of something that was supposedly told to him, I presume - we don't know from the document - by Mr. Kordic. Under those circumstances, we would suggest that the document itself is -- or use of this document is not consistent with the interests of ensuring a fair trial for Mr. Kordic under Rule 89(D), especially at this late stage of the game.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Court can apply its -- take judicial notice and common-sense approach that, in a number instances and various professions, including the military, lawyering, and perhaps sometimes even judging, people -- documents are prepared for some person's signature and signed by someone on their behalf, and I don't think that goes anywhere near to raising a substantial question about the authenticity of the document such that would keep this document from being admitted. The next document is 447.1. Your Honour, this is a report or statement by the chief of artillery of the Central Bosnia zone. It is, frankly, extremely important because this document gives an account of repeated instances in which Colonel Kordic was involved in giving artillery orders. It again covering the period from -- in late January 1993, continuing up until the -- on the direction -- excuse me, Your Honour. I'm looking at the third page, at the bottom of the third page on the translation. On the 4th of February, 1215 hours, Colonel Kordic asked that Dusina and Merdani be processed with the multiple-rocket launcher. Now, the Chamber will see this is an instance where we've talked about in the last two days about how documents interconnect and corroborate each other. If the Chamber looks back at 439.2, the reference -- the order signed for him, that is, Blaskic, is exactly the same order, an order on the 4th of February and using the rocket launcher on the same place, Dusina. So not only do we argue for the admission of Exhibit 447.1, Your Honour, but again, this is exactly the type of instance where the documents are -- mutually reinforce each other. And this is also highly corroborative of the audiotape. The audiotape again talks about Kordic giving artillery orders, and we see him in this document, indeed during that same time period, giving artillery orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This document, Your Honour, is (A) cumulative, and (B) contains many multiple levels of the hearsay. In addition, the very instance that Mr. Scott referred to on the bottom of page 3, it says, "Colonel Kordic asked that Dusina and the village of Merdani be processed but he didn't ask Mr. Batinic," according to Exhibit 439.2. The argument that the Prosecution makes according to Exhibit Z439.2 is that obviously this demonstrates a direct conversation between Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic. So the two documents are not internally consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that's interpretation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, for the purpose of rationally organising the matters, I think that, at the beginning, you should have perhaps told us how many of these documents, beginning with the documents concerning Mr. Kordic, how many documents you're going to tender into evidence. utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the Court will give me the time, I do not have that number. I did not count them. We've done this during the lunch hour so, if you will give me a moment, I will count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I'm curious. I just think that we should have a number for both Mr. Kordic and Mr. Cerkez and we should know if there is, perhaps, a number of overlapping documents which would concern both accused. In this manner, you are going to avoid repetition and having to repeat one and the same thing in respect of a particular document. You should tell us the reasons for one or the other particular category of documents and I think in this manner we will speed up the matter because we are using this precious trial time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, obviously, Your Honour, that's a reasonable question. We'll count the documents now. The duplication with the Cerkez list, we'll try to avoid duplication. Obviously, we are not going to submit the same document twice, but as Mr. Nice and Mr. Lopez-Terres are in the process of doing that at this moment, I'm sorry, I can't -- I'm not in a position to give the Chamber any information on that. This process all relates to the Court's ruling immediately before the lunch break. So we've been working non-stop since 1.00 to try to shorten our list, and I'm sorry, this is as far as we've gotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you doing the counting now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Off of this list, yes, Your Honour. We just did it. Off of this list, Your Honour, which started out with about approximately something over 140, 142 documents, we have selected 49, which, in our submission, is a dramatic reduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as regards the other list?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I indicated a moment ago, I'm not in a position to be able to give that information at this point. We're doing this as we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we speed up and try to finish this process within the hour please, Mr. Scott. It's not a matter of criticism, but we must try to get through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can just read the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I'd like to hear your justification. These are important documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we can speed up in both cases. Also, Mr. Sayers, bear in mind we've seen your objections. So there's no need to repeat them at length. Let's go on to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 455.1. Your Honour, this is a document which, again, talks about the first page of the facts are the following. "For a long time now, HVO soldiers, or rather, 'special units' which are responsible directly to Dario Kordic have been destroying Muslim houses," et cetera. It obviously is talking about the events in late -- well, in January and February 1993. The document also goes on to say, at the top of the next page, the first paragraph on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've got the argument on this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It isn't just so much -- let me just respond. And again, Your Honour, it's hard to take these shortly because it's not just an order, a document about military authority, but it also talks about other issues such as the ones on page 2 leading into this question about the other civilian authorities, the civilian HVO authorities are not functioning at all. That's the only other point I wanted to make about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish you'd look at this document. It's completely anonymous; it's not on any letterhead. Anyone could have written it. We would -- I would respectfully submit that it's ridiculous to propose this for -- as a candidate for admission in a criminal trial, especially on this issue, Your Honour, the connection or the asserted connection between Mr. Kordic and special purpose units, and we just refer the Court to the discussion contained on pages 16 through 18 of our brief for further citations on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Next document is 483.2. This is a report from the securities sector. It talks about, again, issues concerning the roles and positions -- excuse me, roles being played by Dario Kordic, Ignac Kostroman at the top of the second page. We think, again, it goes to the relationships between these people. Towards the bottom of the third -- toward the bottom part of the third page, it talks about special police headed by Anto Sliskovic which was actually kind of a private police of Kordic's and Kostroman's. It goes on throughout talking about Sliskovic, Kostroman and Kordic. Anticipating Mr. Sayers' objection, it appears to be true that it is not signed. However, it's on HVO letterhead. It follows all formats that the Chamber is familiar with in terms of the information. It is an order that bears -- has an order number, the date. It is not simply a blank letter on stationery but has all the indicia of an HVO order, albeit without a signature which, again, a number of HVO orders or documents don't have signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's nothing whatsoever in the nature of an order about this anonymous document which expressly says, "Sources reliable," although we don't know who they are, "Data partly verified." We won't repeat the objections that are contained in our papers, Mr. President, but this is cumulative and absolutely violates Mr. Kordic's right to a fair trial under 89(D) and part 3 of the test that you articulated this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 527.4. Our records show that 501.1 is in now, on further checking, if anyone wants to confirm that or not. 527.4 we submit, again, for the information provided about the -- in the Busovaca Brigade, the references to Mr. Sliskovic telling Mr. Uzunovic, "You have no business interfering in these matters." Sliskovic indicates that, if he wants, he can replace Blaskic and Uzunovic. Mr. Vukovic is related to having complained that 70 per cent of the military police were criminals and looters, and two days after that -- after a meeting, that was at a meeting involving Mr. Kordic and Mr. Kostroman, and two days after these comments about the military police, he was replaced. It also says that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to repeat what we have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure exactly how much to say on these, Your Honour, but that's our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A word or two will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: With respect to this document, Your Honour, the first document is anonymous and unsigned and unstamped. And it has an attachment which is anonymous, unsigned, and unstamped as well. So under the test articulated this morning, the same objections apply to this document as stated to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very briefly, the second document, it's a -- it's the same document, the second one bears, you'll notice it bears the Zagreb archives stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Next one is 544.3. It's a report signed over the name of Dario Kordic, talking about the Vitezovi in March of 1993. There is -- sorry, Your Honour, there is one comment -- I made a note and I don't see it at the moment but this is clearly Mr. Kordic himself giving a report about the activities of the Vitezovi, one of the Special Purpose Units and also bears -- shows a Paket communication information, which is authentication. It also bears the Zagreb archives stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Unsigned, unstamped, and the first page is, according to the person who prepared it, whoever he was, page 2. Also, there's no authentication number up on the top left-hand corner of the Croatian original. Once again, Your Honour, absolutely anyone could have written this and there's no evidence where it came from, where, in the location of the archives it was supposedly produced. So even under the standard, the very liberal and expansive standard articulated by Mr. Prelec today, there is simply no way to figure out whether this document is real or not. And at this late stage in the game and under Rule 89(D), we object to it for the reasons as stated for the previous two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Our response, Your Honour, is that's the first time I've heard that not only do we have to say that it came from the archive but we have to tell from which folder from the archive it came. The next document is 780.2. It's a document from Blaskic to Kordic, asking, essentially, for Kordic's approval or his input on an issue about releasing some detainees also specifically connected to the case and that it involves the Viteska Brigade. So it touches on Mr. Kordic. It touches on the Viteska Brigade and detained persons and Blaskic asking for Kordic's view. It bears a Zagreb stamp and signature and an HVO stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The translation's not correct, Your Honour. It actually says in the Croatian information on the top of the document. With respect to this document it looks like there's a proper signature and a proper stamp and a proper archival stamp. So it may be this document is one of the limited category of documents that looks like it might have existed at one point. And it's up to the Trial Chamber, therefore, we would suggest, to determine what weight to give this document, but it seems to be cumulative. It also seems to be addressed to the Kaonik issue, and we introduced no Kaonik evidence in our case-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we hear whether 501.1 has been admitted or not. It has been admitted. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next is 896.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can deal with it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is a report dated the 9th of May. It talks extensively about the events in Central Bosnia, including some of the conflicts among some of the political authorities which the Chamber has begun to hear more about recently. It's -- it actually contains a great deal of information about what was happening in Central Bosnia at this time. Frankly, it's a very balanced document, arguably says as many -- what might be viewed as positive things from Mr. Kordic as negative things, but in any event, that's our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This document at least has someone who has signed it. The Croatian word at the back of it is "kum," which means "your buddy" in Croatian. That's the person who wrote this document. Multiple levels of hearsay and cumulative and Rule 89 objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Next is 975.2. This is -- this is one of the Ahmici, so-called Ahmici reports by Anto Sliskovic on the 25th of May, and we think that report is clearly relevant to this case and the Chamber should have that in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's already in evidence; 975.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: 975.1, Your Honour. 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next is 1043.1. This is a general announcement to the Croatian people signed by Kordic, Blaskic, Kostroman. I think it contains language that we think is fairly inflammatory, especially in the context at the time. On the second page talking about the Muslim Mujahedin Jihad fanatic hordes that are destroying Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Objection, unsigned, unstamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And cumulative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next is -- so, Your Honour, I might just say again there was only two -- we've only selected two from that page, taking into account one already admitted. The next is 1133.1. This is a letter to Mate Boban from Kordic and Kostroman. Again, a fairly wide-ranging report about events in Central Bosnia at that time. Two particular points, Your Honour. This relates -- this is one of those documents that corroborates, in our view, the report about the -- concerning the four presidents that we've talked about before, the one in February of 1994. I don't have it in front of me at the moment but I believe it's 1367.1 because it talks about some more events in terms of the conflicts with other leaders in the area. On page 3 it also talks about -- Mr. Kordic uses the term "balija pacifism," and if Mr. Sayers tells me the use of "balija pacifism" is cumulative, I would like to know all the other instances where it is used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, that kind of document attributing that kind of comment to Mr. Kordic at this late stage of the game certainly should be signed, and this one isn't. Anyone could have prepared this. Furthermore, it wasn't on the October 30th index provided to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Next.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 1140.7. This is a letter from Valenta to Colonel Blaskic and Colonel Kordic concerning the relation between the civilian and military authorities, and, Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's submission that in addressing this to mister -- Colonel Blaskic and Colonel Kordic, they are the military authorities that Mr. Valenta is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Completely cumulative in addition to the objection stated in our papers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 14 -- excuse me. 1140.6. Some -- very similar letter and the same rationale, Your Honour. It's a different subject matter but it's the relations between military authorities and international organisations. Prosecution submits it's a complaint from Mr. Valenta to the military authorities, that being Blaskic and Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 1144.4. Sorry, Your Honour, sometimes these pages stick together. There is a letter or communication from Mr. Kordic about the Office of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Chamber will recall -- there was a number of instances, a number of different titles and positions, ranks that Mr. Kordic has used. There are other documents talking about the forward office of the president or something, but this is yet another version of the Office of the Presidency which we submit shows the centralisation of authority in his office in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We've objected to this document but it does show the difference between IZM, which is a military title and the izmjesstenos ureda djela predsjednisstva, which has been the subject of previous colloquy between Mr. Kordic's counsel and the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you objecting?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We stand with the objections that we put in our papers, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next is 1147.5. This is a communication written on the -- from the relocated Office of the Presidency from Busovaca on the 20th of July, 1993. It is particularly relevant in reference to page 5, which again reflects and corroborates other documents, including the four presidents' complaint, if I can refer to it in shorthand, that -- saying -- talking about the conflict with Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak, et cetera. Each those of these documents corroborate again each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's unsigned, document's incomplete, no stamp; anyone could have written it. And Mr. Scott may say that there was only one relocated Office of the Presidency but that's a matter of argument and not matter of proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Court will just give me one moment, please. Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. The next document is 1152.3. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think in many of these we can actually read the point that you make. There's no need to repeat it. If that's -- you can just simply refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just -- on that one, Your Honour, I apologise. I'm just having a hard time finding the page. Well, there is a -- the comment, Your Honour, is it may or may not be apparent on the face of it. I can't presume what the Court's view would be. But our point and apart from -- this is -- the Prosecution would submit that a core cadre of people who were around Kordic at that time, most of the -- the Court will recognise many of these names and in argument we would tell you about many more. By looking -- if the Court cast its eyes down this list, we would suggest to the Court that this is indeed a list of the very -- of Kordic's closest lieutenants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was no objection stated in our papers to this and we have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 1181.2. Addressed -- well, addressed, among others, to Colonel Kordic in Busovaca. In particular, it talks about the declaration of the republic as opposed to the Community Herceg-Bosna contrary to various Defence statements about how it was still viewed to be part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it was still a part of the same state and very friendly. Point 2B calls for the end of activity of all Croats and official bodies of the former republic BiH and talks about other points of reference to the developments of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at one previous point in this case you mentioned that you hoped that this was not going to end up as a trial about politics. Well, it appears to have done. This person -- this document is not signed by the person, whoever it is. It's not stamped and it recites multiple levels of hearsay. We would submit that it's of the utmost peripheral significance to this case and is completely cumulative of the mountain range of other evidence on the same points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just briefly respond. Of course it's a political case. It's about political persecution, among other things. 1195.3 is a communication from Ante Valenta to Colonel Kordic, again seeking to -- or excuse me, dealing with -- transporting ammunition from Pula to Vitez, also relates to international armed conflict, references to two helicopters in Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Cumulative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Cumulative in addition to the other objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 1197.4. Letter that -- commending -- from Colonel Kordic, commending the action in Grbavica. The Prosecution will submit, Your Honour, in argument that the actions of Grbavica were not particularly honourable. There were war crimes committed both during and after and our position is that this is incriminating and showing Mr. Kordic commending the action. It bears an archive stamp. It also bears a Paket communication stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is just -- even if it were signed, which it's not, even if it were stamped, which it's not, this document purports simply to be a public commendation for the actions of soldiers, that's all, and it's of the utmost peripheral significance and completely cumulative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, we submit it's not peripheral at all. It goes to the core of the case, this relation, this person commending war crimes. 1201.3 is the next document. utterances.text: But you would -- it may not be invited, but you would not oppose our reopening the question of Mr. Vidak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We wouldn't invite it. We don't think it's necessary. We think the evidentiary inquiry regarding this document really answers itself, Your Honour. But if the Court thinks that it's necessary for this gentleman to return, that's correct, we would not -- right. We would not oppose it. And if I may, we'll just hand out Mr. Vidak's letter for distribution to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we'd object to the statement. We haven't offered his statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter as to whether it's an idea to have him called or not. But, Mr. Scott, very briefly, because we really are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do appreciate that, Your Honour, but Mr. Sayers has gone on at some length about this and even raised Rule 68 violation issues. We have not seen such a letter. If Mr. Sayers, apart from handing to the Chamber, would like to tender a copy to the Prosecution, we're most happy to look at it. It's news to me and to Mr. Nice. We can only say that, in the initial contact that our office had with this witness, and I don't know if his name - I guess it's probably too late now - was completely cooperative. So what's happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The document -- more importantly, Your Honour, let me turn to the document itself. And this is an important document. We've covered this in the paper we filed today. I asked the Chamber to review that with some deliberation in reference to the other documents marked. It is extremely -- it is an extremely trustworthy document when viewed in the light of the huge number of other information. We have listed in that paper a number of other documents that refer to the same things, including letters by Mr. Kordic himself in which Mr. Kordic refers to this conflict. There is other types of evidence than testimony. The reason it was not put to more live witnesses during the trial is because the document came to our attention very late and that is the only reason why it is not featured earlier with other witnesses in the trial. Moving on -- I'm sorry. We -- we do anticipate, Your Honour, that there could be a witness that the Court will be familiar with being received next week which may also shed light on this matter concerning a witness. Next document is 1371.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think from now on we'll just have to have the numbers. We've got written submission on these.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour I'm happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just let me double-check, Your Honour. I'm hesitating, Your Honour. I'm going to say that 1380.4, but I'm not sure if it's the same, if it's duplicative or not at the moment. So 1380.4 so as not to waive any -- that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Z1380.4 I believe is already in evidence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's why I raised it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that's it, Your Honour, but if the Court would give me one second ... Mr. Nice reminds me that on 1356.4, which is not in the binder but was tendered previously, we talked about, we will provide another copy to the Chamber. Your Honour, I believe that is -- the only -- Your Honour, if you'll let me check one document. It seems to be out of order, but ... Well, I'll finish, Your Honour. If the Court will allow me, just before the whole process is completed, to check one item, come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can mention it tomorrow morning and we'll hear the Cerkez documents tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to tomorrow, the witnesses held over from today, I think one of them may have children and she's anxious, I think, to get back. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us the position in the morning and maybe we can make a decision about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we could have the argument about -- if it was convenient to the Chamber to interpose the argument about the transcripts and, if appropriate, to then interpose the evidence, which will not take long, but I'm entirely in the Court's hands. It's under 30 documents for Cerkez, a few for miscellaneous, which I haven't gone through, and the diary that's outstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So that the witnesses are not imposed on unnecessarily or more than necessary, we'll deal first thing with the argument about the transcripts and about the witnesses, the two things really hanging together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of November, 2000 at 9.30 a.m.
